rv.q: Bob Crowley's astonishing designs live up to that description; they gleam, glitter and sparkle like nothing else in the West End.
On the whole this is a show with a well-judged air of mischief and spectacle.
It is all nonsense but it is done with conviction by Casey Nicholaw, the director and choreographer, who bombards us with business.

“There are some breathtaking special effects but the production has an old-fashioned feel as it attempts to combine Broadway razzle-dazzle, the vibe of a typical Bob Hope/Bing Crosby ‘Road’ movie and the stream of cheeky, self-referential humour that flows from Beguelin's script...Amidst the orgy of bling-flashing and scimitar-waving...it's the...
It’s not so much “Never mind the quality, feel the width” as “The width is the quality”.
As for the rest of the show – it’ll keep you ticking over until Christmas, but that's it.
This is a no-expenses-spared stage version of the 1992 kiddies’ cartoon film.
But, for all the visual splendour, spry, yearning-filled lyrics and syrupy sounds, it barely rises above the generic; a cynic’s idea of Disney “magic” at its blandest.
If you're looking for an entertaining and visually striking performance, Aladdin is the musical for you.
Even by West End standards, this is a big and bold production.
But the sheer bravura of the production papers over all the cracks.
If, like me, you love magic kingdom then you’ll love this show.
This is a gleeful evening that stops at nothing to ensure children of all ages enjoy themselves.

cn.t: Critics offer mixed-to-positive reviews for this lavish Disney spectacle, praising its dazzling visuals and standout Genie performance while noting its panto-like qualities and occasional two-dimensional storytelling.
